title: TA8-01124
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, herein called "the claimant", a national of El Salvador and Guatemala,1 seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act", the IRPA.2 The claimant is in possession of a passport from El Savador3 and was born in Guatemala.4 In 1992, the claimant married a citizen of El Salvador and became a nationalized citizen of El Salvador. Counsel indicates the claimant is a citizen of both countries. Allegations

The claimant alleges a well-founded fear of persecution and fears a risk to her life at the hands of her husband, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, herein called "XXXXX". The claimant alleges XXXXX was a XXXXX XXXXX and later XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant married XXXXX in 1992. They have three children born in 1982, 1987, and 1995. After the marriage, the claimant alleges physical abuse including forced sex. The claimant further alleges that XXXXX has a drinking problem and did not support his family. The claimant cited an example of abuse when she was pushed against a wall and a nail entered her back. The claimant tried to leave XXXXX who pushed the claimant to the floor injuring her shoulder. On another occasion when XXXXX came home drunk, he cut the claimant's finger with a machete. The claimant also alleges that XXXXX kidnapped their young daughter. In XXXXX 2003, XXXXX threatened the claimant that he would cut the claimant into pieces and send the pieces to her father. The claimant left the next day and went to live with her father. In XXXXX 2004, the claimant travelled to the United States (U.S.). In 2008, the claimant came to Canada and made a refugee claim on January 17, 2008. Determination
I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. Analysis

In arriving at its decision, the panel considered the issue of whether the claimant's fear is objectively reasonable. In order to do so, the panel considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in El Salvador or Guatemala, whether or not the claimant took all reasonable steps to avail herself of that protection, and whether she has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The panel also considered the issue of an Internal Flight Alternative, where the claimant could live safely without a serious possibility of being persecuted. In arriving at its decision, the panel considered all of the evidence in the context of the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines and the panel accepts that the circumstances which give rise to women's fear of persecution are often unique to women.5 State Protection

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Federal Court and Supreme Court of Canada. These principles, enunciated hereafter, pertained to the case at hand and were accordingly applied.

There is a presumption that, except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown, the state is capable of protecting its citizens. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. A claimant can rebut this presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.6 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must be not only reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.7

No state is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times and the fact that the state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens. That the state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption of state protection.8 It should be noted that less-than-perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.9

Furthermore, the law states that the burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy in that state. In a functioning democracy, such as El Salvador or Guatemala, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show that she has exhausted all courses of action reasonably available to her.10 Moreover, local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.11 Indeed, if a claimant believes the actions of some police officers are corrupt, the onus is on them to approach other members of the security forces or authorities.

The documentary evidence12 before the panel indicates that El Salvador is a constitutional democracy which holds generally free and fair elections. Although the constitution provides for an independent judiciary, the judiciary suffered from inefficiency, corruption and insufficient resources thus undermining the public's respect for the judiciary. The panel, having perused the country conditions documents,13 finds that El Salvador is in effective control of its territory despite the foregoing information, and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country. There is nothing in the documentary evidence before the panel to suggest that El Salvador is in a state of complete breakdown.

More importantly, the National Civilian Police Force (PNC) formed in 1993 is considered by international human rights as a success story. There are several specialized divisions and also territorial divisions. Community law reaches about 80% of the population of El Salvador. The police organization recognises internal problems and is directing efforts by enacting changes to the Organic Law in 2004.14 This documentary evidence states that complaints can be lodged through the government funded office of the Human Rights Defense Attorney (PDDH). The PNC has an internal affairs office called Inspector General (IG) where police misconduct can be registered.15 The attempts to curb corruption within the police have had some success as reported by the General Directorate of Penal Centres (DGCP).16

According to the Department of State report, "violence against and discrimination of women"17 continues to be a problem as supported by further documentation.18 Nevertheless, El Salvador has introduced national laws aimed at protecting women from various forms of discrimination such as The Law Against Intra-Family Violence (1996) which condemns physical, or psychological violence. The penal code (1997) also specifies penalties for domestic violence and sexual harassment. Spousal rape is not yet recognised as a crime. The government recognises the need for legislation to protect women from gender related violence, yet many are critical of the government's application of its legislation into practical application. In an effort to improve its application, many government groups are collaborating with NGO's to combat violence against women through education, increased law enforcement and support of the NGO organizations.

In 1996, the government's Salvadoran Institute for the Development of Women (ISDEMU) set up a program for the improvement of family relations. This national program, which is aimed at female victims of violence, offers women psychological help and social assistance. The program sees about 10,000 new cases each year, provides a telephone hot-line and runs a shelter. In 2008, the ISDEMU added health services including psychological counselling.19

The department of State report on Guatemala provides some background information about gender violence.20 The country is a multi-party republic ensuring free and fair elections. Within the country there are a variety of domestic and international human rights group operating with little government intervention.

Gender related offences remained a serious problem. The law criminalises rape and a 2008 law has established penalties for physical, economic and psychological violence. The police have minimal special training and this weakens the intent of the law. The government had maintained the PNC unit for sex crimes. There is an office of Attention to Victims and an office of the Special Prosecutor for Crimes against Women. Under the law, restraining orders can be issued and police protection provided, yet the police do not fully respond to these laws. The Institute of Public Criminal Defense provides free legal help and medical and psychological assistance. There is a government program for Prevention and Eradication of Intrafamily Violence which received 250 calls daily.21 In 2000, the legislation also passed the Presidential Secretariat for Women and the National Coordinator for the Prevention of Domestic Violence and Violence Against Women.22

Finally, Guatemala is a signatory of the Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) as well as Inter-American Convention on the Prevention, Punishment and Eradication of Violence Against Women. Most recently, a law passed in 2008 now sends men to jail for prosecution for aggression and abuse against women.23

The government of Guatemala, which demonstrates a clear understanding of the required legislation to eliminate gender-relate violence, must now proceed further by providing better services to implement its laws and legislation.24

The claimant was asked what she did in seeking state protection from the violence of her husband, XXXXX. The violence began in 1992 not long after the couple married. The claimant testified that XXXXX had a drinking problem and he would physically abuse the claimant like the time when he pushed her against the wall and a nail pierced her back or another time when he cut her finger with a machete. XXXXX would also force the claimant to have sex. When the claimant tried to leave her marriage, she was beaten by XXXXX. The claimant did not seek medical treatment as XXXXX had threatened her. The claimant did seek advice from a lawyer who advised the claimant to go back with her husband. In 1998, after an argument, XXXXX took their 3 year old daughter away to San Salvador for three days. The claimant did file a police report of kidnapping but XXXXX returned and he was not arrested as the claimant wished. The abuse continued into 2003 and the claimant finally left with her children to live with her father. Shortly after, the claimant travelled to the U.S. where she lived illegally until 2008.

I have great sympathy for the predicament of the claimant but I cannot accept a claim of a lack of state protection, as the claimant only once made a police report and that had nothing to do with the years of alleged abuse by XXXXX. A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.25 One visit to the police to file a complaint over a period of twelve years of abuse does not provide for "all reasonable steps," therefore, the panel discounts the claim of a lack of state protection.

The claimant also testified that XXXXX was a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant contends that she fears his connection with the authorities and consequently was reluctant to engage the state. The adequacy of state protection cannot rest on the subjective fear of the claimant.26 A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.27 Again, the panel determines that the claimant did not fulfill her responsibility of providing probative evidence for her lack of engaging the state for protection and, as such, is discounted as credible.

The panel recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is adequate state protection in El Salvador and Guatemala and the police are both willing and able to protect such victims of gender violence.

The panel is satisfied that were the claimant to return to either El Salvador or Guatemala and seek protection from authorities for any violent acts perpetrated against her, protection would be reasonably forthcoming.

The panel finds that the claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. Therefore, this panel is not convinced that the countries of El Salvador and Guatemala would not be reasonably forthcoming with state protection, should the claimant seek it. Internal Flight Alternative
I will now turn my focus to the issue of Internal Flight Alternative.

The panel finds that the claimant could live in the city of Quezaltenango, Guatemala without a serious possibility of being persecuted.28 The city has a large population and is considered a principal town of the country of Guatemala. I have considered the educational level of the claimant and conclude that, in a city of this substantial size, the claimant could secure work. After several years of separation, the persecutor is not likely to venture that far from his home state of El Salvador to find the claimant. If the persecutor has not been able to locate the claimant for the last seven years, it is unlikely he will be able to locate the claimant in Guatemala.

The panel is guided by the Federal Court in assessing whether a viable IFA exists. If there is a safe haven for the claimant in her own country, where she would be free of persecution, she is expected to avail herself of it before seeking safety in Canada unless the claimant can show it is objectively unreasonable for her to do so.29 The IFA must be realistic, attainable and accessible. Barriers to getting to the IFA must be reasonably surmountable and the claimant cannot be required to encounter great danger or undergo undue hardship either in travelling there or in remaining there. A claimant cannot reject an IFA for frivolous reasons, such as not liking the weather. In law, the fact that a claimant may be better off in Canada economically, physically and emotionally than in her own country, is not a factor to consider when assessing the reasonableness of an IFA.30 If a viable IFA exists, a claimant is not then a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

The leading case on IFA directs the panel to use a two-pronged test in considering cases where a potential IFA presents itself.31 First, the panel must be satisfied that there is no serious possibility of persecution in the part of the country in which the IFA is located. If the panel is satisfied of this, then secondly, the panel must further consider whether or not it would be unreasonable in all circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, to seek refuge there.
The claimant always bears the burden of proof to show that there is a reasonable chance that persecution will occur in the entire country and specifically in the potential IFA named.32

Although the claimant has not lived in Guatemala for over forty years, she testified that she could earn a living by selling products in a market and would be able to find accommodation. The claimant's negative comment to the suggested IFA in Guatemala was that she has concerns for the over-all crime and violence. The claimant also has a sister who lives in Guatemala City. By the claimant's comments, the member is satisfied that it is reasonable for the claimant to relocate to the identified IFA.

The claimant also stated that she could not live in the location suggested, as XXXXX will not give up until he finds her. The panel accepts the claimant's subjective fear of her persecutor. Nevertheless, the claimant has been unable to provide credible evidence why relocation is not an option as her ex-husband has not located her since she left him in 2003. The claimant lived with her father for a year from 2003 to 2004 before she traveled to the U.S. Although the claimant was not asked if she had any interaction with XXXXX during that year, the silence of any documentary evidence or testimony would indicate that he did not find her during that time. Also, since the claimant's departure from El Salvador in 2004, the claimant has never been located by XXXXX and indicates only a recent visit to her father by XXXXX in 2009. The addition of this added information was part of an amended Personal Information Form (PIF).33

The member recognizes that the claimant will face challenges as she relocates to Guatemala, but is assured by the claimant's comments of her ability to secure work and accommodation even with her limited education. The history of the claimant points to a person who, in the face of difficulties, was self-sufficient and provided for herself and her family while in El Salvador and also supported herself for four years while living in the U.S.

The claimant's rejection of Quetzaltenango is based solely on her fear of being found by XXXXX. The claimant provided rational why this could occur: XXXXX has contacts with the military and the police in El Salvador from past employment; XXXXX could bribe people to obtain information on her whereabouts; XXXXX has threatened that he will never give up until he finds the claimant and finally, the amended PIF indicates that XXXXX is still looking for the claimant as recently as 2009. The member rejects all of the above rationale put forward by the claimant. As the claimant, through her testimony, indicates that XXXXX does not know she is in Canada at present, she has not provided any probative evidence of XXXXX alleged capability of using police or military contacts or bribes to locate her. The amended PIF is dated XXXXX XXXXX, 2010. The member questions why the claimant waited over a year to add this information since she was aware of XXXXX visit to her father as early as XXXXX 2009. The member rejects this information as credible as it appears as an afterthought in order to embellish her claim. As such, it is not considered credible.

The panel should note that the countries of El Salvador and Guatemala have admitted to a problem of domestic violence but have demonstrated an effort to confront this issue by establishing significant legislation cited above and recognizing the need to bolster the implementation of the legislation.

While there are some noted inconsistencies among sources, the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that the city of Quezaltenango in Guatemala is a potential IFA for a claimant alleging persecution. Although the claimant has not lived in Guatemala since she was five years old, the claimant does have a sister residing there. The panel accepts that the claimant would be moving to a strange location with little support, yet the claimant has accomplished the same two times before when she moved to the U.S. in 2004 and when she moved to Canada in 2008. I conclude it would not be unduly harsh for the claimant to relocate there. Testimony of the Witness

The claimant called her sister, XXXXX XXXXX, who is a permanent resident of Canada. The witness confirmed she was aware of the abuses of her sister's husband as the claimant related her problems through a few telephone calls. Documents provided confirm the family relationship of the claimant and XXXXX XXXXX as her sister.34 CONCLUSION

The panel considered all of the documentary evidence, including the testimony of the claimant and witness, observations, and submissions, relevant provisions of the IRPA and the jurisprudence on which this panel has relied. The panel concludes that there is adequate state protection for the claimant in El Salvador and Guatemala and that furthermore, she has a viable IFA in Quezaltenango. For the same reasons the panel finds that, on a balance of possibilities, she would not be subjected to a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture if she were to return to Guatemala or El Salvador.
In accordance with section 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA, the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person at risk of harm.

Therefore, the Refugee Protection Division rejects her claim. (signed) "C. Wedgbury" C.
